title: Don't call the scriptures false
hook: don't call the Vedas and the Semitic books false; false is the one who doesn't reflect (Prabhati, Kabir, ang 1350)
tomorrow: I am the worst of all

segments.voice: Yesterday, Brahmin, and your line, born the same way. Did you greet someone you'd usually pass by? Today Kabir turns from birth to books. Day seven hundred fifty-three.

Two shelves. On one, the Vedas, the old hymns of the Hindu tradition. On the other, the Kateb, Kabir's word for the books of the Muslim neighbors, the Qur'an among them. A weaver who has just told a proud man that birth makes no one higher might be expected to sweep both shelves onto the floor. If caste doesn't count, maybe the books don't either. That's not what he does. In a hymn in Raag Prabhati, Kabir draws a line in a very different place. Today: don't call the scriptures false.
screen: `TWO SHELVES.` → `THE VEDAS AND THE KATEB.` → `A LINE IN A DIFFERENT PLACE.`

segments.voice: Kabir's hymns in Raag Prabhati sit close together on the page. One opens wide. First, Kabir sings, God made the light, and from that one light the whole creation came. So who is good and who is bad? Then, in a neighboring hymn, comes the line in today's title. Don't say the Vedas and the Kateb are false, he says. False is the one who doesn't reflect. Read that twice, because it moves the problem. The danger isn't sitting on the shelf. It's sitting in the reader. A book can be read with care or with no thought at all. Someone can carry a holy text everywhere and never once stop to think about what it asks. Kabir points his finger there, not at the pages. And notice what he isn't saying. He isn't saying all books say the same thing. He isn't asking anyone to give up their own. He's naming a habit: dismissing a scripture you haven't sat with, or reciting your own without letting it reach you. Both skip the same step. The word in the line is bichar, to reflect, to think something through. Sikh teachers say the Guru's word asks to be understood, not only recited. Read that way, Kabir's line asks the same of every reader, whatever shelf they read from: sit with a line before calling a book empty, and let your own book reach you before calling it full. That's today's carry: reflect, don't dismiss.
screen: `FROM ONE LIGHT, THE WHOLE CREATION.` · `FALSE IS THE ONE WHO DOESN'T REFLECT.` · `THE DANGER SITS IN THE READER.` · `BICHAR: THINK IT THROUGH.` · then, large: `REFLECT, DON'T DISMISS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: reflect on one line of any scripture. Your own, a neighbor's, one you've only heard quoted. Settle, and breathe. Bring one line to mind. If none comes, use today's: false is the one who doesn't reflect. Say it slowly, inside. Then ask it one question: what is this asking of me today? Don't argue with it, and don't rush to agree. Just turn it over, the way you'd turn a stone in your hand. If you pray, you can say Waheguru before and after. The bell holds the time.
Bichar. To reflect, to think something through: Kabir's word for the one thing a reader of any scripture owes it before calling it empty.
Your line: reflect, don't dismiss. Today, when you're about to wave off an idea or a book, give it one honest minute of thought first. Day seven hundred fifty-three.

screen: `DAY 753 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: I AM THE WORST OF ALL.`

howItsDone: Sikhs sing this Prabhati hymn of Kabir in kirtan, and Sikh teachers use its line on the Vedas and the Kateb to call listeners to reflect on scripture rather than dismiss anyone's.

fork.setup: you're Kabir. you've just told a proud man that birth makes no one higher. now someone asks: so are the holy books false too? what do you say?
options: don't call them false; false is the one who doesn't reflect.
only my own book is true.
fork.reveal: Kabir moves the problem from the page to the reader: the false one is whoever doesn't reflect.

original.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi: reflection, thinking something through. Kabir's line turns on it.

trapdoor: what you thought: a saint who rejects religion's books.
what it means: Kabir says don't call the Vedas or the Kateb false; the false one is whoever doesn't reflect.
what a scholar hears: the line moves the problem from the text to the reader, and it sits near a hymn that opens with all creation coming from one light.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Raag Prabhati, Kabir, Ang 1349–1350 (from one light, all creation; 'don't say the Vedas and the Kateb are false; false is the one who doesn't reflect')

notes: Hymns paraphrased; confirm Ang 1349 (one light) and Ang 1350 (Bed/Kateb line) as separate Prabhati hymns.
Kateb glossed as 'the books the Muslim neighbors honor' (the index says 'the Semitic books'); no etymology given. Confirm gloss.
The same hymn goes on to question a mullah's practice; deliberately left out so another path is not made the foil.
'Sikh teachers say the Guru's word asks to be understood, not only recited' is a general claim; confirm or soften.
Gurmukhi ਬੀਚਾਰ (the line's spelling may be ਬਿਚਾਰੈ, verb form); confirm noun spelling and 'bee-CHAAR'.

Editor: the 'one light' opening (Aval Allah noor upaaiaa, Ang 1349) and the Bed/Kateb line (Ang 1350) are separate Prabhati hymns; teach, myth and trapdoor no longer present them as one hymn. Dropped 'Punjabi' as the line's language.

Audit: Kateb gloss tightened to 'Kabir's word for the books of the Muslim neighbors, the Qur'an among them' (Kateb is usually read as the Semitic scriptures, so not the Qur'an alone); the teach's closing 'before you call a book empty...' recast as what the line asks, not a direct instruction to the listener.
